name: Subject-Linked Genitive Superlative

1.definition: Presents the performance at an extreme on a scale associated with the subject.
1.details: In worked our hardest, our refers to the people doing the work and hardest characterizes their effort. The postverbal expression has no overt noun and supplies a degree or standard. A linked at-pattern is available with some verbs. Its range differs, as in be at one’s best. The label objoid in the cited work notes the position and the unusual object profile. The present entry leaves the grammatical function of the bare phrase open.

examples.form: Kate and I have [worked our hardest] to raise them that way.
examples.note: COCA example in CASA. Our is linked to the subject.
Published comparison with the separate at-pattern, using the same verb.
Published illustration of the bare variant.

relatedConstructions.notes: The superlative supplies a degree standard.
The examples have no overt noun after the superlative. The head analysis remains open.

grounds.note: Documents conventional collocations and productivity from COCA.
Distinguishes the bare and at-patterns and provides corpus examples.
Reports asymmetric priming and discusses what this can support about their relation.

projection.target: The genitive normally tracks the subject while the bare superlative supplies a high degree for the performance. A related phrase with at can broaden the interpretation to a condition.
projection.evidence: Bouso’s corpus analysis and CASA’s contrasted records. The published priming study reports an asymmetry between the two forms.

curious.title: Worked our hardest
curious.summary: A verb followed by a genitive and a superlative, as in worked our hardest, says the effort reached its highest point.
curious.body: In worked our hardest, the word our points back to the people doing the work, and hardest describes their effort. There's no noun after hardest. The phrase supplies a degree, a standard of how hard. A version with at is also possible with some verbs: They worked at their hardest. The two don't have exactly the same range. Be at one's best is another at-pattern. This dictionary marks the analysis as provisional and leaves open what grammatical role the bare phrase has.

examples.text: Kate and I have [worked our hardest] to raise them that way.

curious.try: Say They worked their hardest and They worked at their hardest. Do they feel the same to you?

teacher.summary: Optional enrichment on worked their hardest and the related at-pattern.
teacher.explain: The pattern is a clause with a subject and a verb followed by a phrase whose genitive is linked to the subject and whose superlative sets a high degree: our refers to those doing the work, and hardest characterizes their effort. The postverbal expression has no overt noun. A linked at-pattern is available with some verbs, with a different range (be at one's best). The cited work uses the label objoid for the position and unusual object profile. This dictionary leaves the grammatical function of the bare phrase open, and the head analysis is open, so avoid presenting one analysis as settled.
teacher.terms: Objoid is the label in the cited work. This dictionary leaves the function of the bare phrase open.

examples.text: Kate and I have [worked our hardest] to raise them that way.

contrasts.note: The at-pattern, with the same verb.

watch_for: A learner might look for a noun after hardest, when the phrase has no overt noun.
A learner might read our or their as owning something, when it tracks the subject.
teacher.activity: Students complete They worked ___ hardest and We tried ___ hardest with the matching genitive for each subject. They check that the genitive refers to the people doing the work.
